title: James Blake - Breaking and Entering
summary: Mercury Award winning, Grammy nominated artist James Blake phoned into Breaking and Entering to chat with Simon and Lauren about his latest album 'Assume Form'; covering topics such as mental health (for which James has become a vocal advocate in recent times), love, masculinity, vulnerability and how this album represents him finding peace.
transcript:
English singer-songwriter, musician and producer James Blake spoke by phone with Simon Winkler and Lauren Taylor in January 2019, shortly after the release of his fourth album, Assume Form. They discussed love, writing more direct lyrics, vulnerability and the pressures of touring. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: 'CMYK' by James Blake was a landmark when it arrived in 2010. There was a real surge in experimentation in dubstep, post-dubstep and hybrid styles incorporating R&B, electronica and heavy synth sounds, and James quickly established himself as one of the leading figures. His contemporaries were the xx and Mount Kimbie, both of whom he's collaborated with numerous times over the years. In the years that followed, he became a go-to collaborator, working with Kendrick Lamar, Beyoncé, Vince Staples, Frank Ocean, Mount Kimbie and Bon Iver, amongst numerous others. He has released four albums now. The latest, Assume Form, came out just last week.

Lauren and I were fortunate to speak with the Mercury Award-winning, Grammy-nominated artist about the new record. We spoke about mental health, for which he's become a vocal advocate, how this album represents him finding peace, and masculinity and vulnerability.

Lauren: We've had James on the show a couple of times over the years. The last time we spoke was in 2013, around the release of Overgrown. Since then it would be almost impossible to count the collaborations he's been part of. Simon, you mentioned a few earlier: Beyoncé, Kendrick Lamar, Jay-Z, Mount Kimbie and Frank Ocean. Collaborations are reflected on Assume Form too, including André 3000, Rosalía and Moses Sumney, a good friend of James's. They've worked closely together, toured together, and James has remixed one of his songs.

We begin the interview talking about Moses Sumney's album Aromanticism, which talks about romantic love and questions expectations and experiences of love. We asked James what place romanticism has in Assume Form.

James: In the case of this record, I am in love. I think romance is definitely different to love; we can separate the two terms. I think this record is a romantic record, and it is so because of my relationship. I just tried to put the ideas as simply as possible and say exactly what I meant.

Simon: James, can we talk about your process with Assume Form? How did these new songs start to assume form?

James: I think my lyric approach changed on this record. I'd been struggling a little bit to place myself lyrically and understand why I wasn't maybe getting the satisfaction out of lyrics that I was hoping for. There is always a really great moment if you write something down that feels like it sums up everything you feel about a situation, or the commentary rings true, authentically, with how you feel. Then there comes this satisfaction, and I felt like for the first year of writing I wasn't getting that.

I had a conversation with my girlfriend about it, and she said, sometimes you don't always just say what it is you're thinking. You sometimes mask it in some abstract, clever way. I really took that on board and tried to just say the thing. After trying to do that, I ended up writing songs that really spoke to me. Hopefully they speak to other people, but at least I felt the satisfaction of having achieved that for myself.

Simon: We were struck last year when the singles for this album started to be released, including 'Don't Miss It'. The lyrics are very direct. It seems to form a mantra, a direction or at least a suggestion to be present in your own life in a more active way. Is that a fair assessment of what you hoped to communicate?

James: Yeah, 100 per cent. I think it's a monologue of a neurotic, anxious, egocentric person. I heavily identified with that description at the time. I think maybe it's advice to people who are going through that. Far be it from me to impart wisdom onto the world, but that situation and headspace really lost me so many years of love and life.

I can't remember a lot of the great things that happened in my 20s because I was so wrapped up in myself, worrying about what people thought of me, the comparison between the artist and the person, and how I could ever live up to the perfect avatar that had been created. I know I have different problems to some of my friends and to other people, but I think the essence is to say you can lose the best years of your life by worrying. It's a kind of plea with people, in a way, not to let that happen.

Lauren: James, when 'Don't Miss It' was released as a single last year, you responded to reviews and critiques with thoughtful comments about vulnerability and masculinity. Would you share what you were communicating and what response you received?

James: Other than reading it out, I don't know if I could sum it up better than I did, because I thought about my wording quite carefully. But the gist is that I didn't want people to be dissuaded or discouraged by the stigma on emotional vulnerability in music. Because the tag was specifically 'sad boy', I spoke on how it's affected me. I think statistically we can all agree that that is something that heavily affects men. But I think overall, everybody, every gender, suffers from repression via conditioning. The conditioning, I think, comes from people's stigma and the way we're brought up.

That particular article I linked was just an example. It wasn't the only time that's happened. In fact, that publication has been printing stuff like that for years and years and years about me. I was like, God, really? This is what you're going to come back with? Jesus. I'm trying to make the best shit I can make, and this is how you're going to dissuade people from listening to it. I tried to put myself in the shoes of a listener as well and go, if I read this, I'm not sure if I'd feel that cool for listening to it.

Lauren: James, alongside music, you've contributed greatly to awareness and understanding around mental health. The last time we spoke in 2013, the level of touring and travel you were doing was really extreme. Only if you feel comfortable discussing this, what have been the biggest changes you've made that had the most positive impact on your mental health and general wellbeing?

James: I stopped touring, for a start. In the grand scheme of things, my touring was not that extreme. I was just suffering mentally, and I think any touring was making it harder. If you look at the tour schedules of some artists, it's fucking crazy. Because streaming has made it almost impossible for us to make money out of record sales, we have to go out and play live shows to sustain ourselves as musicians.

Some people are luckier than others. I was lucky, I am lucky, and I come at this from a privileged position, not only now, but even when I started. I didn't have the absolute survival necessity to go out and make money, because I could have stayed with my parents or whatever. My music career really kicked off in exactly the way I was hoping it would. I really got to do whatever I wanted, and I was glad to do that because I didn't have that financial pressure. It's different for everyone, from whatever economic background you come from.

In a general sense, I think touring puts pressure on already sensitive people. People who write and perform music very often experience great sensitivity to the world and can be overstimulated. I think people who go into it are already vulnerable to mental health issues, and that is shown in the statistics for suicide amongst musicians. I spoke at a conference recently about suicide amongst musicians, and it's something like four times higher than in the general population.

I think the factors that contribute to that are obviously being away from home. It's hard to keep up relationships, whether that's friendships or love or whatever. It's almost like going to space, and you come back and everybody's aged at a different rate. It's very difficult to explain what you've just done to people, so it can be quite isolating. People are expected not to complain. We think because we get to do this thing, we shouldn't talk about how we feel, because it's stigmatised. You're a musician, you get to do something really cool, so don't complain.

The other thing is when you learn to express yourself through music, not through words or confrontation or the normal channels of communication, and that's financially rewarded, you get into this loop of, well, this is what makes me money, so this is what I'm going to continue doing as my main method of expression. That's all anyone expects from you, so you carry on not communicating any other way. Not everyone does, but certainly I did, and I know a lot of people who've done this. There's not much support in the way of professional advice or help while you're away. If you're someone who needs to survive by touring, or needs touring to survive, then you're not going home, you're not getting the professional help you need. You're basically at home for about two days to wash your clothes, then you're back out on the road in this bubble. It's a strange and perfect storm for mental health.

I think things are changing slightly. There are things people can do, people are helping. Lots of artistic people are turning to meditation and things to deal with stress and whatever they're going through. I think we could help musicians more, whether it's therapists at festivals, on the road, whatever, things they don't have to fork out more money for that could help them while they're away.

After saying everything I said about touring, I haven't had it the hardest out of all the musicians I know and in terms of the general musician population. I think I've had a pretty easy ride, to be honest. I've enjoyed immensely a lot of the moments on tour, and I think it's an amazing occupation. I feel so lucky to be where I am, to almost wake up at 30 and go, I'm so happy with where I am. I love the record I've made, love the people I've collaborated with, and I'm extremely grateful for everything that's happened. If I can help people on the touring circuit with anything I say, then that's great, but I think we probably need professionals.

Lauren: Thank you, James, for your thoughtful answers today, and congratulations on the new album. It's been a pleasure to speak to you.

James: It's great to speak to you too, and I can't wait to come to Australia.
